elements.quote: Despite accumulating evidence of its diagnostic accuracy over the last decade, scepticism regarding its clinical effectiveness and cost‑efficiency continues to hinder widespread acceptance. ... Research indicates that keeping FERs under 30% is essential for encouraging patients to prefer CCE over colonoscopy. ... Despite its significance, a systematic review of FER in CCE remains absent.
elements.reason: The introduction outlines the existing knowledge (diagnostic accuracy, cost‑efficiency concerns) and highlights the key uncertainty—the lack of a systematic review of follow‑up endoscopy rates.

elements.quote: The follow‑up endoscopy rate (FER), which encompass procedures like colonoscopy or flexible sigmoidoscopy, greatly influence the economic viability of CCE. In addition to its economic effects, FER influences patient experiences and environmental sustainability. ... This systematic review and meta‑analysis aim to evaluate FERs and identify factors influencing these rates to support the effective implementation of CCE.
elements.reason: The passage explicitly explains why the review is needed: FER impacts cost‑effectiveness, patient experience, and environmental sustainability, justifying the conduct of the review.

elements.quote: Despite its significance, a systematic review of FER in CCE remains absent.
elements.reason: The authors state that no prior systematic review on FER in CCE exists, so the conditional requirement to discuss existing similar reviews does not apply.

elements.quote: The primary aim of the review was to evaluate the FER following CCE. The secondary aims include exploring contributing factors to the FER to guide future research to reduce this rate further.
elements.reason: The review focuses on diagnostic performance and follow‑up rates, not on the effects of an intervention; therefore, describing a mechanism of action is not applicable.

No logic model or hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes are presented in the introduction, and the review does not involve a complex intervention requiring such a model.

elements.quote: The primary aim of the review was to evaluate the FER following CCE. The secondary aims include exploring contributing factors to the FER to guide future research to reduce this rate further.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states its primary and secondary objectives in the Methods section, fulfilling the requirement for an explicit statement of review objectives.

elements.quote: The primary aim of the review was to evaluate the FER following CCE.
elements.reason: The review does not assess comparative intervention effects (e.g., CCE vs another intervention) and therefore does not require a PICO‑style statement of planned comparisons; the conditional element is not applicable.

elements.quote: The search included full-text clinical, retrospective, and prospective trials evaluating the use of CCE in patients with any colonic pathology... Both adult and paediatric studies were considered, provided they offered clear documentation of follow-up investigations after the initial CCE.
elements.reason: Study designs and follow‑up requirements are described, but settings (e.g., geographic or clinical setting) are not specified, so the element is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: The electronic search covered studies published between January 2004 and August 2024... There were no language restrictions, and all the non‑English articles were screened with the intention of being translated and included if they met the predefined inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: Eligibility criteria for report characteristics are clearly stated, including publication year range, language policy, and exclusion of conference abstracts and other publication types.
The manuscript does not report a distinction between exclusions because outcomes were not measured and exclusions because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Metaregression was performed, analysing prespecified subgroups or covariates, including capsule type, different CCE indications, age, sex, and the proportion of participants with adequate bowel cleansing (%) and complete transit rates (%).
elements.reason: Groups used in each synthesis (e.g., capsule type, indication categories, age, sex) are explicitly specified and relate to the review’s secondary objectives of exploring factors influencing FER.

elements.quote: Exclusion criteria primarily focused on studies where follow‑up investigations were conducted for upper GI findings, as these conditions would not typically be identified during colonoscopy, the gold standard for comparison of CCE FERs.
elements.reason: Provides a clear rationale for the notable restriction excluding upper‑GI studies; additional rationale for excluding conference abstracts is given in text_6.

elements.quote: The sensitivity analysis using both leave-one-out analysis and filtered out the two high- risk studies showed consistent effect size estimates across all iterations. No single study disproportionately influenced the overall results (see online supplemental figures A2 and A3), demonstrating the robustness of the meta- analysis.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports that sensitivity analyses were performed and describes the overall pattern of results (consistent effect sizes, no single study influence), but does not provide detailed numeric results for each analysis, so reporting is incomplete.

Certainty is not communicated alongside the reported results in any section‑appropriate format.
No evidence summary tables such as GRADE Summary of Findings tables are present in the retrieved material.

elements.quote: The pooled FER in our study was 42%, which appears relatively high when compared with benchmarks in related procedures like colonoscopy and CTC. ... In the context of CTC, cost‑effectiveness is significantly reduced when FERs exceed 30% (16). ... When compared with these benchmarks, the 42% FER in our study underscores the need for targeted strategies to mitigate factors contributing to this high rate.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly interpret their pooled follow‑up endoscopy rate by comparing it with existing evidence and benchmarks from colonoscopy and CT colonography, thereby situating their results within the broader literature.

elements.quote: Finally, this study has several limitations. The first is the high heterogeneity in the results. Despite applying meta‑regression and subgroup analysis, heterogeneity remained substantial. This was primarily driven by multiple confounding variables within each covariate, including the lack of a standardised bowel preparation and booster regimen, variability in CCE indications, differing exclusion criteria, and inconsistencies in national referral thresholds due to variations in guidelines... In addition, CCE indications were not consistently documented across all included studies, and subgrouping them during the meta‑analysis process may have introduced bias. Furthermore, the limited number of studies, particularly within subgroup analyses, may have reduced statistical power, preventing definitive conclusions.
elements.reason: The discussion section explicitly enumerates several limitations of the evidence (high heterogeneity, inconsistent bowel preparation, variable indications, inconsistent documentation, limited number of studies), satisfying the requirement to discuss limitations of the included evidence.

elements.quote: Finally, this study has several limitations. The first is the high heterogeneity in the results. ... This was primarily driven by multiple confounding variables within each covariate, including the lack of a standardised bowel preparation and booster regimen, variability in CCE indications, differing exclusion criteria, and inconsistencies in national referral thresholds due to variations in guidelines ... In addition, CCE indications were not consistently documented across all included studies, and subgrouping them during the meta‑analysis process may have introduced bias.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly lists several limitations of the review process (high heterogeneity, lack of standardised bowel preparation, variability in indications, inconsistent documentation, potential bias).

elements.quote: Despite applying meta‑regression and subgroup analysis, heterogeneity remained substantial... The limited number of studies, particularly within subgroup analyses, may have reduced statistical power, preventing definitive conclusions. ... These challenges ... may have introduced bias and affect the reliability of the pooled estimates.
elements.reason: The same paragraph explains how each limitation (heterogeneity, limited study numbers, inconsistent documentation) impacts the review’s conclusions, statistical power, and risk of bias.

elements.quote: Addressing these issues is essential to enhance the clinical efficiency, patient experience, and cost‑effectiveness of CCE.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly outlines how improving completion rates, bowel preparation, and patient selection will affect clinical practice, indicating clear practice implications.

elements.quote: Professional guidelines in the US and EU recommend KPIs of >95% for caecal intubation rates and >90% for adequate bowel preparation. The Royal College of Radiologists in the UK recommends a reinvestigation threshold of <25% as a KPI.
elements.reason: The passage references existing professional guidelines and KPI thresholds, reflecting policy implications for the use of CCE.

elements.quote: Future research should focus on improving completion rates, bowel preparation protocols, and refining CCE indications. This will minimise environmental impact and enhance cost‑effectiveness and patient satisfaction.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly recommend specific areas for future investigation, providing clear recommendations for future research.
